newsitem.title: USA: Federal trial begins for Arizona governor.
newsitem.headline: Federal trial begins for Arizona governor.

text.p: Jury selection began Tuesday in the federal trial of embattled Arizona Gov. Fife Symington, who faces fraud, extortion and perjury charges that could end his career and send him to prison.
Seven prospective jurors were questioned in the morning session in U.S. District Court and all were placed in the final pool from which 12 jurors and five alternates will be selected.

Federal Judge Roger Strand overruled two challenges by Symington's defence attorney John Dowd, who questioned one man and one woman about their answers to a questionnaire that appeared to be biased against the governor.

Symington, a colourful, 51-year-old Republican, faces 22 felony charges. Federal prosecutors will try to prove to the jury that Symington committed fraud, extortion and perjury in connection with real estate deals during the last decade.
If convicted on even a single count, the two-term governor will be booted from the office he has held since 1991. He also faces a possible prison term.

Questioning of prospective jurors Tuesdsay focused on three areas: how panellists felt about bankrupcy and whether it would colour their view of Symington; whether the rich and powerful should get a break from the justice system; and what were their views on labour unions, the apparent target of Symington's alleged extortion.

During the trial, expected to last 12 weeks, prosecutors will detail what they claim are lies told by Symington from the mid-1980s to the early 1990s, when he was a developer, to secure credit lines and business and personal loans.

The government contends Symington made false statements to lenders to prevent his real estate empire from crumbling. Prosecutors also will try to prove Symington extorted an agreement from six union pension funds to release him from a personal loan guarantee he made to obtain a $10 million loan for a shopping centre in downtown Phoenix.
Lastly, the government will try to prove that the governor lied under oath during court proceedings when he filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy in September 1995.
The charges stem from a probe into the 1989 collapse of Southwest Savings & Loan Association. Symington served on the thrift's board of directors.
After settling the case, the U.S. Attorney's office in Los Angeles continued its probe into the governor's financial dealings for several years. Last June Symington was indicted.
Since then, there have been calls for his resignation by Arizona's largest newspapers, and his popularity in public opinion polls has slipped to 30 percent.
Symington, a descendent of industrialist Henry Clay Frick, has repeatedly maintained his innocence and has said he plans to seek re-election in 1998.
He has told the people of Arizona that he can continue to carry out the duties of governor while attending the trial four days a week.
